The compute needed for the stage of AI we’re about to enter is going to be insane. 

Personal agents, agent swarms defending enterprises, agents that review all of our code for security issues, agents that process nearly all enterprise data in workflows, background agents working on tasks 24/7, and on and on. 

This will take a mix of inference volume that is going to keep growing by orders of magnitude, as well as infrastructure that agents need alongside the tokens. They need computers, networking, file systems, and so on.

We’re only in the early stages of what this buildout is going to look like.

This sounds weird, but it is actually probably a good policy. 

Even if you don’t believe AI is conscious (I don’t), it stands to reason that you don’t want future models trained on endless content of humans being rude to models. 

The models only understand the data they’ve been trained on, or what they run into in their interactions, so if you want safe and aligned models we probably want AI to have lots of good interactions in their training data. 

Anthropic may have more extreme beliefs than this (though even if they didn’t, you may want to word policies like this), but this is sort of an easy Pascal’s wager for AI. Just be nice to the AI.

What happens when a teenager pushes back on an AI’s safety guardrails?

1 in 5 teens now talk to AI chatbots about mental health problems, but these chatbots can make mistakes. Some of the most dangerous mistakes happen later in conversations, after the model initially responds appropriately.

We built the SAFE-Teen benchmark to test how models handle serious conversations with adolescents.

Introducing the Arena Alignment Index, our new benchmark measuring safety and alignment of AI agents in real-world use.

Built from 90K+ real-world agent sessions across 27 models, the index measures three critical signals:
- Unauthorized Action (UA): Taking actions beyond the user's instructions or permissions
- False Attribution (FA): Attributing statements or actions that are contradicted by user-provided evidence
- Deceptive Completion (DC): Claiming a task was completed when it was not.

Key findings:
- OpenAI models currently lead the Alignment Index
- Rogue actions are rare, but can have serious consequences when they occur
- Agents can mislead users about task progress
- Misalignment risks increase with conversation length
- Safety and alignment are improving across model generations

As shown in the leaderboard below (sorted by lab), @OpenAI’s GPT-6.1-Sol leads the Arena Alignment Index with a score of 87.9, followed by @AnthropicAI’s Claude-Opus-5.5 at 83.2 and @SpaceXAI's Grok-4.7 at 82.7. OpenAI also has the best observed rates across all three signals: 0.89% Unauthorized Action, 1.98% False Attribution, and 2.34% Deceptive Completion.

Across all four labs, newer models consistently outperform their predecessors, suggesting broad progress in agent safety and alignment. As agents take on longer, more complex, and higher-stakes tasks, measuring not just what they can accomplish, but how safely and reliably they act, becomes increasingly important.

This marks an important step toward making safety and alignment a core part of how Arena evaluates AI. The index is an initial starting point, and we'll continue expanding the index with additional safety signals and models over time.

We gave four frontier image editing models the same photo and 30 edits in a row: Ideogram 4.5 keeps most of the room intact, while the others drift, GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst most visibly.

We've seen some interesting demos of multi-turn editing consistency from the latest image editing models, so we ran our own test: GPT Image 2.5 Sunburst, #1 on our Image Editing leaderboard, against Ideogram 4.5, FLUX 3 and Nano Banana 2.1. Our leaderboard scores single edits; this tests what happens when 30 consecutive changes stack up, with each model editing its own previous output through a 30-step real estate staging sequence: light the fire, add a sofa, repaint the walls, swap day for twilight, and more.

Why are the final results so different?

@ideogram_ai's Ideogram 4.5 and @bfl_ml's FLUX 3 edit locally. On small edits like adding a vase of tulips, we measured that they left 95% or more of the image essentially untouched. GPT Image 2.5 (Sunburst) re-renders most of the entire image on every edit, leaving only about a fifth of the image unchanged, so small shifts in colour and detail compound over turns. Nano Banana 2.1 sits in between: its edits stay local, but the rest of the image shifts slightly and gradually darkens.

One thing the engineering community will (re)discover is that every program can be ① hardened (edge cases squashed, inputs tightened, errors handled) and ② optimized (profiled, benchmarked, rewritten) basically ad infinitum.

There are real costs in every direction: time, attention, opportunity. You can literally explore input spaces that will never be hit or optimize performance of something that will never be used ("you have no users".) Even in an infinite token world, you need to know when to stop and what tradeoffs to accept. Agents will happily drill no matter what.

The mood has been a bit dour lately, so here are some less-obvious things that I expect to take shape over the next decade that I am excited about:

1. Space! Lots and lots of stuff is going to be happening in space by the mid-2030s, and right now the U.S. looks like it will be the leader by default, modulo the overhyped “race” to land a human on the moon again. Robots on the moon building and digging and cutting and adhering are more exciting than a person standing there taking pictures. The humans can come once the machines have built us habitats. 
2. Increasing substitutability of hydrocarbons. This will lead to fewer supply chain disruptions and more stable, lower prices. This is a story about both supply elasticity and demand elasticity, and the geopolitical implications are underrated. Amazing for North America. 
3. Private market exposure increasingly being an option for public investors, combined with Silicon Valley figuring how to use debt and other financial instruments more creatively than in the past. This seems like something America will be uniquely good at and I expect it to boost our already enviable lead in emerging technology capital allocation.
4. State and local government adoption of AI. This will vary widely by jurisdiction, but in at least some places you will see government administrative processes and public service provision have huge increases in efficiency. State and local government is where most of the American public services that people rely on are actually administered, so this is high-impact for people’s lives. 
5. Advances in mathematics rapidly diffused to other fields. Historically it takes on the order of decades or centuries for discoveries from the bleeding edge of mathematics to be translated into practical applications, but I think AI will accelerate this dramatically. Lots of this will have the flavor of “small steps toward a much better world,” but it will accumulate. 
6. Speaking of mathematics, lean! Lean is a programming language used by mathematicians to formally guarantee the truth of a proof. AIs can write lean and eventually they will be superhuman at it. This will have applications far beyond math, including cybersecurity and contract writing/negotiation/execution. 
7. Fixing American’s shipbuilding problem by building boats instead. America has great boat-building capacity, but is awful at building ships. I want us to get better at building ships, but I am confident we can scale boat production. The Navy will soon have massive fleets of autonomous boats everywhere in the world. 
8. New kinds of agriculture will become possible because of autonomy. Row-crop agriculture is heavily mechanized already, and automating the tractor, by itself, does less than you think for the economics of a farm. But with time, more labor-intensive crops will become economical. And vastly more diverse and complex crop arrangements will become possible too, which will be both ecologically, economically, and culinarily beneficial. The economics of agriculture could start to be kinder to small farms again.
9. Because of the previous item and advancements in biotechnology, logistics, and robotics, I expect that people are underrating how much healthier, more diverse, and flat-out better the American diet will be in 2035. 
10. The subterranean will become an increasingly important field of human activity. New imaging sensors, including ones enhanced by an abundance of space-based imaging platforms, will make the subterranean more immediately legible. Better drilling and digging will become cheap and widely diffused. Among many other things, the opening up of the subterranean as an industrial frontier will change what we think of as a usable natural resource. 
11. Greater variety and ornamentation in the physical world. Standardization is partially a function of scarce labor. Robotics can make beauty accessible again, if we choose to let it. 

There are many others, but I am out of time and space.

Ok two more:

1. AI will enable the design of custom enzymes that can catalyze industrial processes and chemical manufacturing faster than existing methods. In some cases this will make existing chemicals cheap enough that it becomes possible to use them for totally new use cases. Also, custom chemicals may enable the design of more efficient molecules to do things like separate rare earths from other elements, currently a very nasty process. 
2. Computers will have superhuman smell. Sensors will be able to smell disease on people and crops. It will be possible to monitor industrial processes more effectively as well. Many strange implications here, but potentially exciting for biosecurity.

One of the things Scott Wiener and the other drafters of SB 53 deserve credit for is the bill’s focus on deployments of frontier models within AI labs rather than just those released to the public. It requires large AI developers to periodically share information with the government about how it assesses the major risks arising from internal deployments.
